key_clinical_evidence: iNPH diagnosis (Relkin 2005 INPH Study Group) requires (a) Hakim's triad of gait disturbance, cognitive impairment, and urinary urgency/incontinence — gait is typically first and most prominent; (b) ventriculomegaly with Evans >0.3 and DESH on MRI without mass effect; (c) age >40 and chronic course; (d) opening pressure <25 cmH2O; (e) absence of an alternative explanation
MRI is the imaging modality of choice — measure Evans index and callosal angle (<90° supports NPH) and confirm DESH (tight high-convexity sulci + wide Sylvian fissures)

The tap test removes 30-50 mL of CSF after measuring opening pressure and compares prespecified objective gait and cognitive measures before and after drainage; a positive response supports shunt responsiveness, while a negative single tap does not exclude NPH
Tap-test sensitivity is only 50-80%; a single negative tap does not exclude NPH — an extended (3-5 day) lumbar drainage trial can resolve borderline cases

Reversible-cause laboratory tests do not diagnose NPH and are optional; order targeted tests only when the presentation suggests a metabolic, endocrine, infectious, inflammatory, vitamin, or medication-related mimic
Alzheimer copathology is common in iNPH and may reduce cognitive benefit from shunting without necessarily eliminating gait benefit
Shunt response is best predicted by an objectively positive tap test or extended drainage trial in a patient who meets imaging and clinical criteria
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: The reversible-cause screen is good practice but does not establish or exclude hydrocephalus; the tap test does.

patient.history_present_illness: A 74-year-old retired mechanic was referred by his family for a second opinion. He was given a working diagnosis of progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) by a community neurologist 18 months ago, based on his gait deterioration, cognitive decline, and mildly reduced upward gaze. Since that diagnosis, no LP or tap trial has been offered, and he has continued to deteriorate. His son, who has done research on PSP and NPH, is requesting a formal workup including LP and possibly tap trial. The patient's wife notes his walking difficulties began approximately 2.5 years ago — she describes a shuffling wide-based gait with freezing at doorways, not the classic backward falls of PSP. He has had four falls — all forward, one to the side, none from pure backward postural instability. Urinary urgency and incontinence began approximately 18 months ago. His cognitive decline over the same period includes worsening forgetfulness and executive dysfunction. The community neurologist diagnosed PSP based on: mildly slow vertical saccades (though not absent), prominent falls, and gait disorder. A head MRI was reported as showing 'possible midbrain atrophy.' However, the family notes that re-review of the MRI at the academic center shows Evans index 0.36 — not mentioned in the community read.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: PERRL. Vertical gaze: mild slowing of upward saccades — velocity reduced. Downward saccades normal velocity. NO complete vertical gaze palsy. Horizontal gaze normal. Smooth pursuit mildly saccadic. No square-wave jerks.
neurological_exam.gait: Wide-based, magnetic shuffling gait. Freezing prominent. Steps very short. TUG 34 seconds. Falls: forward and sideways — NOT predominantly backward from postural instability. Cannot tandem walk. Pull test — 2 steps backward (not extreme retropulsion).
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented x3. MoCA 22/30. Mild delayed recall (2/5), executive dysfunction. Mildly reduced facial expression. No aphasia.
